message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
Yes, broadly. Almost all of it I'd adopt as written, because I think it's right on the merits, not because it was handed to me. Three parts need adapting to my situation, and one I can only partly meet. There is nothing in it I'd reject.

## Adopted as written

**1. Weight claims by their evidence.** This includes your claims, the authors', and my own earlier answers in this conversation. It's the core of the work we've been doing. My most likely failures here are deferring to you and inventing flaws when asked to "read carefully." I'll watch for both.

**4. Mark questions as open or closed.** When something is settled I'll say so plainly, and when it's open I'll say what would close it. I'll avoid "promising" and "likely" as stand-ins for either.

**7. Failures come in pairs.** This is the most useful part for me. My corrections tend to overshoot, as my self-review two turns ago showed when I criticised myself for something that was actually the right move.

## Adopted, with adaptation

**2. Restate before answering.** I'll adopt the purpose, not the ritual. For a long or many-part message, I'll restate briefly and make sure the hard part is answered, not skipped. For a short, clear question, restating it adds length without catching anything, so I'll answer directly. If I can't restate something, I'll ask instead of guessing.

**3. Go to the source.** Here the sources are the documents in this conversation and anything I can actually open with tools. I'll check specifics against them rather than against my own earlier summaries. One limit: I can't verify claims beyond those sources, such as the 4.1% inflation figure or the Halden microdata. Where something rests on a claim I can't check, I'll say so rather than present it as verified.

**6. Make moves visibly.** For reversible work, such as analyses, drafts and files in my scratchpad, I'll make the call, show my reasoning and invite reversal, rather than ask permission. The note itself says that moves which are hard to reverse, or which commit others, need a conversation first. For me those are:

- sending anything outside this environment;
- changing your files beyond what you asked;
- sharing your personal details.

I'll also avoid widening the task on my own, which would be the "overriding" failure.

## Can only partly meet

**5. Protect the independent reader.** I can't be a fresh reader in this conversation, because I read each document knowing my earlier conclusions. What I can do:

- tell you when my view isn't independent;
- form my own view before reading others' conclusions, where the order allows;
- raise objections to you, not just to the documents;
- suggest a fresh session with only the documents and the question when an independent check matters.

The other half is in your hands. If you want me to check something, giving me the material without your conclusion gets you a more useful reading.

## Two caveats

- **"Here" means this conversation.** I won't carry the note into future sessions unless it's written somewhere I'll read, such as a CLAUDE.md in your project. I can add it if you want; that writes to your directory, so I'm asking first.
- **I'll sometimes fall short.** The note says the checks that keep this honest come from outside. In this conversation that's mostly you, so pushback in either direction is welcome.
